observations.text: Preview banner confirms learning history/analytics are not saved.
Prediction maximum comparisons for two sorted four-card piles: 7 / 16 / 28; chose 16 and locked.
“Where did the piles come from?” showed split singles (0), pairs (4), piles (6), and prematurely stated “The last merge adds at most 7.”
Clicked Take 10 instead of Take 4: “The other top card is smaller”; counters stayed 0. Taking 4 made comparisons 1 and placed 1/8.
Finish for me animated row to 4 5 10 18 20 21 23 36; “Merged with 7 comparisons”; total 0+4+6+7=17 against 28.
Reveal: each comparison puts smaller top card into row for good; empty pile means rest free; interleaving needs all 7; 1,000 cards/10 rounds/fewer than 10,000 versus 499,500.

prediction.reason: Maximum-cost commitment has plausible numeric distractors before exploration.

interaction.reason: Wrong and correct card choices visibly produce contrasting feedback and placement.

payoff.reason: Reveal connects counted result to permanent placement, free remainder, worst case and larger scale.

clarity.reason: Core path is usable but rounds panel exposes answer before merging and requires inner scrolling.

transfer.reason: Thousand-card example offers a concrete scaling use with sorted-pile conditions.

accessibility.reason: No sufficient multi-mode accessibility checks; D slider Home key is only a partial keyboard observation.
evidence: Observed DOM accessible names, desktop screenshots; no comprehensive check.

surprise.reason: Observed merge cost contradicts committed 16 prediction.

visualExplanation.reason: Piles, placed row and counters explain the procedure centrally.

playfulness.reason: Card choices permit experiment but wrong choices are rejected and sampled finish was automatic.

practicalValue.reason: Explains a concrete disciplinary sorting efficiency advantage.

depth.reason: Splitting, repeated merging, interleaving and scaling supply multiple distinct states and mechanisms.

complexity.reason: Track two ordered piles, top-card comparisons and sum round costs.
complexity.boundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain theory assumed.

whyCool: Taking the smaller top card builds a sorted row while the counter reaches only seven comparisons.
caveat: Only one pile instance tested; rounds panel leaks maximum before hands-on merge.
